summary: Specifies an IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option that records the minimum Path MTU along the forward path from a source to a destination. The recorded value can be sent back to the source in a return Path MTU field. It is an experimental specification.

eli5.summary: Packets can only be as big as the narrowest tunnel on the route. This lets each router note the narrowest spot as the packet passes so the sender learns the biggest size that fits.

questions: how to discover path mtu with an ipv6 hop-by-hop option
what is the ipv6 minimum path mtu option
how does the ipv6 minimum path mtu option work
how do hop-by-hop options record mtu information
subtitle: Recording the minimum path MTU with an IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option

tldr.problem: Path MTU Discovery often fails on the modern Internet because intermediate routers drop packets instead of sending error messages, and some deployments intentionally block ICMP.
tldr.mechanism: This IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option lets each router record the smallest link MTU it sees as a packet traverses the path, and report it back to the sender without relying on ICMP messages.
tldr.outcome: Applications can discover the actual path MTU in a single round-trip instead of over many probe attempts, potentially improving both performance and reliability.

today: RFC 9268 is an Experimental specification for the Internet community. It was published to allow evaluation and implementation experience. The mechanism shows promise for data center and controlled network deployments where path MTU varies, but wider Internet deployment remains limited due to middlebox filtering and the historical resistance to Hop-by-Hop Options. Progression to Standards Track would require documented deployment experience.

sections.title: The Path MTU Discovery Problem
sections.content:
The Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) of a network link is the largest packet that can be sent without fragmentation. On the Internet, different links have different MTUs. The path from a source to a destination may traverse links with different MTUs, and the bottleneck is the smallest one, called the path MTU.

Senders need to know the path MTU to avoid sending packets that are too large, which would either be fragmented (hurting performance) or dropped silently. The traditional Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) mechanism, defined in RFC 1191 for IPv4, relies on intermediate routers sending ICMPv4 'Packet Too Big' messages when they encounter a packet that exceeds their link MTU. However, this mechanism has known problems: some routers do not send these messages, some deployments block ICMP, and some middleboxes filter or rate-limit ICMP messages. This can lead to a phenomenon called 'black holing' where packets are silently dropped.
sections.eli5: Imagine sending packages through a mail system where you don't know which doors are too small. The post office is supposed to tell you if your package got stuck, but sometimes they don't. You have no way to know what size is safe.

sections.title: How the Option Works
sections.content:
This RFC defines a new IPv6 Hop-by-Hop Option called the MinPMTU option, which contains two key fields: the Min-PMTU field (16 bits) and the Rtn-PMTU field (15 bits). The sender initializes the Min-PMTU field with the MTU of its outgoing link and sets an optional R-Flag to request a response.

As the packet traverses the network, each router configured to process this option compares its own outgoing link MTU with the current Min-PMTU value. If the router's MTU is smaller, it updates the Min-PMTU field. When the packet reaches the destination, the Min-PMTU field contains the smallest MTU along the entire path. If the sender set the R-Flag, the destination sends a response packet that includes the MinPMTU option with the Rtn-PMTU field set to the path's minimum MTU, allowing the sender to discover this value in a single round-trip.
sections.eli5: Each post office stamps the smallest door size it has on your package. At the end, the recipient looks at all the stamps, writes down the smallest size they saw, and mails that back to you. Now you know the safe package size.

sections.title: Router, Host, and Application Behavior
sections.content:
Routers that support the option compare the incoming Min-PMTU value with their outgoing link's MTU. If the link MTU is smaller, they overwrite the Min-PMTU field with the smaller value. Routers must not modify the Rtn-PMTU field or R-Flag.

Sending hosts include the option in probe packets (not all packets in a flow) to minimize overhead. When the option is included, the host fills Min-PMTU with the MTU of its outgoing link and optionally sets the R-Flag to request a response. The host may also include previously cached Rtn-PMTU values to accelerate discovery.

Receiving hosts that see the option with the R-Flag set will typically include the option in a response packet, setting Rtn-PMTU to the minimum MTU they observed. Applications using this option should pair it with methods like RFC 8899 (DPLPMTUD - Datagram Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery) to actually confirm that the path supports the discovered size before using larger packets.
sections.eli5: The sender puts the option on a test package. Routers update it if they have a smaller door. The receiver reads it, notes the smallest size, and sends back a message with that size. The sender can then try sending packages that size.

sections.title: Performance and Practical Benefits
sections.content:
Traditional PMTUD can require many round-trips to discover the actual path MTU, especially when paths have multiple successive links with lower MTUs. This causes long discovery delays and hurts application performance. The MinPMTU option can complete discovery in a single round-trip by collecting information passively as the packet traverses the network.

The option is particularly valuable for data center deployments and paths with mixed MTU sizes. It complements other Path MTU Discovery methods rather than replacing them: applications can use it as a hint to bootstrap DPLPMTUD, avoiding many unsuccessful probe attempts. For high-bandwidth applications, the ability to use larger packet sizes (like 9000-byte jumbo frames instead of the minimum 1280-byte IPv6 default) can significantly improve throughput by reducing packet-per-second processing overhead.
sections.eli5: Instead of trying door sizes one by one, you learn the smallest size from one trip. If you later try a bigger size and get stopped, you know to go back to what you learned.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Since the fields of the option can be modified by any router on the path, attackers could forge packets with false Min-PMTU or Rtn-PMTU values. Applications using this option must validate the packet containing the option before using the reported MTU value. This requires the upper-layer protocol (TCP, UDP, QUIC, etc.) to confirm that the packet is authentic and comes from the expected endpoint.

Transport protocols that use randomized ephemeral ports, IPsec, or TLS provide this validation. DPLPMTUD provides additional robustness by requiring a probe packet to actually succeed (receive a response) before updating the PMTU, rather than trusting the option's value immediately. Additionally, some middleboxes may drop packets carrying Hop-by-Hop Options, so applications should avoid using the option on packets carrying application data, preferring to use it only on dedicated probe packets that can tolerate loss.
sections.eli5: Someone could forge a message saying 'the smallest door is huge,' and then send a package that gets stuck. You need to confirm by actually sending a test package that size and getting a response back.

sections.title: Limitations and Deployment Notes
sections.content:
The option relies on routers being configured to process it. Older routers or those without explicit configuration will silently ignore it. This means the Min-PMTU value may not reflect the true path MTU if a router on the path does not support the option. Additionally, some middleboxes (firewalls, intrusion detection systems) may drop packets carrying Hop-by-Hop Options, a practice that remains surprisingly common on the open Internet.

This option is best suited for controlled environments like data centers where both routers and hosts can be configured to support it, or as a complement to other discovery methods. The RFC itself is Experimental, and progression to a Standards Track specification would likely depend on real-world deployment experience showing its benefits and acceptable compatibility with deployed middleboxes.
sections.eli5: Old mailhouses won't understand the stamps. Some security checkpoints might refuse to deliver packages with the stamps at all. This works best when you control both ends and the middle.
